question: After five rounds of corrections a policy draft keeps regaining problems that were already fixed, and the chat has become hard to follow. Which two steps should the author take? Select two.
options: A) State plainly which parts of the current draft are settled and must be left untouched.
B) Ask Claude to look back through the chat and remember all corrections made so far.
C) Start again with one prompt gathering every agreed requirement in one place.
D) Carry on with more rounds, since each round has been fixing at least one real issue.
E) Change to a different topic briefly and then return, to give the draft a fresh start.
correct_answers: A) State plainly which parts of the current draft are settled and must be left untouched.
C) Start again with one prompt gathering every agreed requirement in one place.
explanations: Correct. Protecting the settled sections is a distinct move from restating requirements: it constrains what may change, which is what stops regressions.
Asking for recall does not resolve corrections that conflict with each other, and it leaves the requirements spread across many turns rather than stated once.
Correct. Consolidating scattered corrections into one clean specification removes the contradictions that accumulate across a long thread of piecemeal edits.
Fixing one thing per round while breaking another is not progress. Continuing the same loop simply repeats the pattern that produced the problem.
A change of subject does not reset anything about the draft. It adds more material to an already cluttered conversation without addressing the cause.
